To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the maximum activity of the radioisotope secreted into milk during the first 48 hours after injection was in the order of 2% of the injected activity for OIH and 0.7% of the injected radioactivity for MAA.
the maximum amount of radioactivity secreted by the mother into milk in the first 24 h following injection was 2.4% for OIH, 0.7% for MAA and 0.22 for HSA.

the secretion of radioactivity into mothers' milk after lung scanning, renography and placental localization with 131I labelled tracers is low and the radioactivity is at its maximum in the first 24‐hours following injection.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the amount and form of radioactivity in human milk after the injection of 131I labelled radiopharmaceutical tracers.
the amount and the form of radioactivity in human milk after lung scanning, renography and placental localization with 131I labelled tracers.
the amount of radioactivity secreted by mothers' milk after lung scanning, renography and placental localization.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the radioactivity secretions into the milk are small, but that they may become clinically significant if a high activity is administered, or if the excretion is high.
the radioactivity secretions in the milk after administration of the three tracers studied were small and of no clinical significance.
in the case of MAA the amount of 131I in the milk is so small that it is of no clinical significance.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
1.5 to 2% of the administered radioactivity is secreted into milk during 24 to 48 hours.
the secretion of radioisotopes into the milk after the administration of labelled tracers is very low.
the secretion of radioisotopes into mothers' milk after the administration of radiolabelled tracers is small and that the radioactivity is at its maximum during 24 hours following the injection.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the amount of radioactivity secreted by the mother in her milk is very low and is unlikely to cause any harm to the infant.
the radioactivity secretions from the radiopharmaceutical tracers used in nuclear medicine procedures are low and do not exceed 2.4% of the administered activity.
the amount of radioactivity in human milk is very low and that the risk to the nursing child is negligible.
